name: Corner Mate
summary: A rook checks along the back rank while a knight guards the king's flight and its own pawns wall it in; Ra8 mates the king cornered on h8
intro: The corner mate is a checkmate delivered by a rook on the back rank against a king shut into the corner. What makes it work is a knight that guards the one flight square the corner leaves open, together with the king's own pawns, which seal the squares in front of it. In the diagram the black king sits on h8, hemmed by its pawns on g7 and h7, while the white knight on e7 covers the g8 escape. A rook lift to the eighth rank finishes the job.
boardCaption: White to move: the black king is cornered on h8 behind its g7 and h7 pawns, the knight on e7 covers g8, and Ra8 delivers the corner mate.

sections.heading: What the corner mate is
paragraphs: The corner mate is a back-rank mating pattern for the specific case where the king is jammed into the very corner of the board. A rook delivers check along the edge rank, and the king, already at the corner, has almost nowhere to go. The single diagonal escape that a corner would normally offer is taken away by a supporting knight, and the king's own pawns close off the rest.

It is a compact, economical mate: one rook does the checking while a knight and a couple of friendly pawns do the fencing. The knight is essential because it reaches the one square a rook on the edge cannot cover, the square diagonally in front of the king. In the diagram every element is in place, so White needs only to bring the rook to the eighth rank with check.

sections.heading: The mating move
paragraphs: White plays Ra8, sliding the a1-rook all the way to the eighth rank. It gives check to the black king on h8 straight along the back rank. Nothing stands between the rook on a8 and the king, and Black has no piece able to interpose on the eighth rank: the pawns on b7 and c7 cannot step sideways, and the knight belongs to White. The check must be met by the king alone.

Now count the king's squares. g8, the diagonal flight in front of the corner, is guarded by the white knight on e7, so the king cannot slip out there. g7 and h7 are occupied by Black's own pawns and are unavailable. The king cannot capture the checking rook, which sits far away on a8. With no flight, no block, and no capture, Ra8 is checkmate in the corner.

sections.heading: Recognising and using it
paragraphs: To steer for a corner mate, watch for an enemy king boxed into a corner by its own unmoved pawns, exactly the h8 king walled in by g7 and h7 here. Such a king has made no luft and depends entirely on the corner's diagonal escape. If you can plant a knight that covers that escape square, as the e7-knight covers g8, the mate needs only a rook with a clear route to the back rank.

For the defender, the lesson is about luft and about that one escape square. A king cornered behind its own pawns is in danger the moment an enemy knight reaches a square covering its diagonal flight; from then on any check along the back rank can be fatal. Making a small escape hatch in good time, or challenging and removing the covering knight, is the way to avoid being mated in the corner.

keyIdeas: The corner mate is a back-rank checkmate against a king trapped in the very corner of the board.
A rook checks along the edge rank while a knight covers the corner's one diagonal flight square.
The king's own pawns seal the remaining squares, leaving it no escape.
Here Ra8 checks the h8 king, the e7-knight guards g8, and the g7 and h7 pawns do the rest.
The king cannot block the check or capture the distant rook, so Ra8 is mate.
Defend by making luft in time or by removing the knight that covers the escape square.
